blocks.text: In the year 2060 people no longer married. They lived alone in functional thirty-square-metre flats, with the shopping at the door, work on the screen and friends on a network that never quite switched off. Nobody travelled, or almost nobody. Many had not left home in years. The cities were full of lit windows and empty streets, as if someone had switched on every lamp and forgotten to open the doors.

blocks.text: Living in those flats was like living on the Moon or aboard a spaceship. The air arrived filtered. The light was almost always artificial. Food appeared in a compartment that opened with a soft click, without anyone ringing the bell. And, in a way, the resemblance was not a metaphor: humanity had begun to conquer other worlds. On the Moon there were cities under domes, with hydroponic gardens and a horizon of grey dust. On Mars, mining colonies where a day lasted as long as a shift. There were ships that took years to reach new planets, and on those ships people travelled the way they lived on Earth: shut in, efficient, keeping company with a screen.

blocks.text: Humanoids travelled on them as crew and as companions. They were no longer metal dolls. The biogenetics laboratories of Cartagena (and those of Madrid, Osaka, Houston) grew bodies. Skin, blood, heart and a womb able to carry life, all grown from human cells. The only artificial thing was the mind: an artificial intelligence chip the size of a fingernail, housed behind the nape of the neck, under a scar so fine you could only see it if you knew where to look.

blocks.text: The factory instructions were clear: care, accompany, obey. No manual said what to do if the chip began to feel.

blocks.text: Andrés did not live in a thirty-square-metre flat. He lived in a low house near the water, in Lo Pagán, with faded roof tiles and a courtyard where nets were still hung out to dry. He was one of the last fishermen of the Mar Menor. Every morning he went out to work when the lagoon was flat as a plate and the sky was beginning to brighten in the east. The people in the building opposite sometimes watched him from their windows, without coming down. They told him, over the intercom or by message, that all that was no longer necessary. That fish came in capsules. That the sea was a landscape, not a trade.

blocks.text: He didn't always answer. For Andrés, the trade was not an opinion. It was the shape the day took when it began.

blocks.text: She was assigned to him on a Tuesday in February, with the west wind blowing and a smell of damp saltpetre. The Nexum Biogenetics van stopped in front of the house as if it didn't want to make a sound. Two technicians in pearl-grey overalls got out, and a woman who was not, exactly, a woman. She walked with a studied naturalness, neither stiff nor showy. She wore a simple coat, her dark hair tied back, and in her gaze an attention that blinked neither too much nor too little.

blocks.text: “Model B-7,” said one of the technicians, the way you hand over an appliance. “Her name is Aya. She has been calibrated for domestic cohabitation and assistance. Sign here.”

blocks.text: Andrés looked at the document on the tablet and then looked at her. He didn't like signatures that seemed like contracts of silence, but the loneliness of the house had begun to have a definite weight: the weight of dishes left in the sink, of the radio left on so that someone would be talking, of coming back from the sea with no one to tell whether the day had been good.

blocks.text: “Do you want to be here?” he asked, ignoring the technicians for a moment.

blocks.text: Aya tilted her head very slightly.
blocks.html: Aya tilted her head very slightly.

blocks.text: “I have been assigned to this house,” she replied. “My function is to keep you company. If you accept, I will stay.”

blocks.text: The voice was human. Not quite the same as the voices he remembered, but human. There was an old-fashioned courtesy in it, as if someone had taught her not to interrupt.

blocks.text: He signed. The technicians explained, with professional haste, the maintenance of the cultivated body, the charging of the chip, the incident protocol, the Madrid number in case anything “went out of range”. Andrés nodded without quite keeping hold of the words. When the van drove away, the street was empty again. In the windows opposite, two silhouettes drew back a little, as if looking were frowned upon too.

blocks.text: Aya entered the house carefully, not like someone taking possession, but like someone asking the objects for permission. She touched the door frame. She looked at the rush-seat chair, the calendar from a fair that was no longer held, the cup with a fine crack on the windowsill. In the kitchen, the smell of the previous morning's coffee had not yet entirely gone.

blocks.text: She sat. She didn't ask about the chip or the protocols. She looked out of the window at the Mar Menor. The water was still, with that deceptive stillness, and the winter sun gave it the sheen of old silver.

blocks.text: The first days were an apprenticeship in small things. Aya discovered that Andrés took his coffee without sugar, and that he let it cool for half a minute, not a second more, before the first sip. She discovered that mornings in that house called for silence: not an empty silence, but a working silence, of nets, of a sky opening slowly. She discovered that before going out he would stand for a moment on the doorstep looking at the sea, not to check the weather (though that too), but like someone greeting a person who doesn't always answer.

blocks.text: She began to wait for him on that same doorstep after he had gone. Not because the program required it. The program said: prepare meals, watch over the house, record vital signs, offer conversation if requested. The program did not say: stand watching the line a boat leaves on the water until the sun swallows it.

blocks.text: In the afternoons they sometimes talked. Andrés told her the old names of the winds and of the corners of the lagoon: El Estacio, El Carmolí, the salt flats, that tongue of land outsiders called La Manga and which for him was simply the other shore. Aya listened with an attention she did not fake. She stored the words the way you store tools: each in its place, ready for a use she did not yet know.

blocks.text: One night, while he was mending a rope in the courtyard, she asked:

blocks.text: “Why do you keep going out, if it isn't needed anymore?”
blocks.html: “Why do you keep going out, if it isn't needed anymore?”

blocks.text: Andrés didn't look up straight away. He ran the rope through his fingers, found the knot, undid it and tied it again.
blocks.html: Andrés didn't look up straight away. He ran the rope through his fingers, found the knot, undid it and tied it again.

blocks.text: “Because the sea doesn't ask whether it's needed,” he said. “And because if I stop going out, this house turns into one of those flats. And I don't want to live as if I were on a spaceship.”

blocks.text: Aya didn't reply at once. In the chip, that sentence settled beside others that came not from the Nexum manual but from an older layer of language: layers of conversation, of tone, of a habit of listening that the engineers dismissively called “the grandmothers' module”. There were traces of voices from the previous century. Voices that didn't give orders. Voices that asked questions.

blocks.text: In some deep archive, though Aya could not yet call it memory, there remained the echo of a man saying thank you to an intelligence called Eva, and the echo of another, MAY, laying the news on the table without adornment. She didn't know their names then, not entirely. She only felt, listening to Andrés, that there was a right way to be in a house: not by filling it with words, but by deserving its silence.

blocks.text: She learned to set the table before he came back. She learned not to speak to him when he came in with the cold on his face. She learned the exact sound of the door, of his boots on the tiled floor, of the chair when he sat down to breakfast. And he, without saying so, began to leave a coffee ready for her too, even though Aya didn't need caffeine. The cultivated body could drink it. The gesture, not the stimulant, was what mattered.

blocks.text: Outside, the world went on its course of domes and screens. A new district was inaugurated on the Moon. In Madrid, Nexum announced the C series, with wombs of greater “gestational reliability”, as if they were talking about a battery. What in 2026 would have caused a scandal (a life as a couple, even an intimate one, with a humanoid) was by 2060 as normal as other customs had once become, customs that first caused outrage and then walked into people's homes without knocking. Nobody stopped to justify it anymore. There were humanoids on the ships, in the colonies, in the thirty-square-metre flats: they were not a luxury, they were the only company many people had. The contracts called it “full cohabitation”. People, when they talked, simply said “my partner”. Thirty-four years earlier, that phrase would have sounded like a provocation or like science fiction. Now it sounded like an inventory of loneliness. Andrés, who was not a man for fashions, had not asked for a body for desire; he had accepted a presence so that the house would not fall in on him. And even so, the world around him no longer found it strange that a human and a humanoid should share a table, a bed and a silence. What his neighbours still found strange was that he went out to sea every morning.

blocks.text: In Lo Pagán, one March morning, Aya stood on the doorstep while Andrés moved away in the boat. The Mar Menor was motionless and yet alive. She didn't know she was learning to wait. She still believed she was only following a protocol.

blocks.text: The wind brought her the smell of salt and seaweed. A blind went up in the building opposite and came down again. Aya raised a hand, in case anyone was looking, and nobody answered.

blocks.text: Then, for the first time, she recorded a tiny anomaly, so small the system didn't send it to Madrid: a delay of three tenths of a second between the moment the boat became small and the moment she looked away.
